processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu (at.%, x = 17) ingot produced from raw materials of high purity (>99.9 %).
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Aging at 575 °C for 10 h, followed by water quenching.

characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 575 °C aging series of the 17Al alloy the hardness rises from 438.1 ± 39.3 HV (1 h) to a peak of 924.9 ± 25.8 HV (6 h) and decreases to 831.3 ± 27.4 HV at 10 h.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and averaged
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the Vickers hardness of the aged 17Al alloy to track the aging hardening behavior (Table 3 / Fig. 2).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al alloy at 575 °C the precipitation of β-Mn accelerates with temperature; the 575 °C / 10 h panel shows a uniform β-Mn matrix.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: SE imaging of electrolytically polished samples (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol), 50 µm main-field scale bars
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the precipitation of secondary phases (α-Mn, β-Mn) and the progression of the α → β-Mn transformation during aging of the 17Al alloy.

characterization_methods.key_findings: Both α-Mn and β-Mn diffraction peaks were found, indicating α-Mn and β-Mn co-precipitated during aging before the α matrix fully transformed to β-Mn.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: 2θ range ~20–110°; the 17Al trace shown is for the 575 °C / 1 h condition
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify constituent phases (α/D0₃, α-Mn, β-Mn) in the aged 17Al alloy.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: GeminiSEM 300 SEM, scanning step size 1.5 µm (low magnification) and 0.05 µm (high magnification)
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al alloy, the α matrix progressively transforms to β-Mn with increasing aging temperature/time, and new BCC and FCC precipitates appear within the β-Mn.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Electrolytically polished samples; phase maps with legend BCC (red), α-Mn (blue), β-Mn (green), FCC (pink/magenta)
characterization_methods.purpose: Clarify the microstructural origin of the rapid aging hardening by tracking the α → β-Mn transformation and new precipitates.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: FEI Talos F200X microscope equipped with an EDS detector, operated at 200 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: Fine FCC Cu-rich particles containing FCC twins are distributed at the β-Mn interfaces; the β-Mn/FCC Cu-rich interface was imaged by HRTEM (characterized on the 575 °C/6 h peak-hardness condition).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Ion-thinned TEM foils; SAED and HRTEM/FFT analysis
characterization_methods.purpose: Elucidate the microstructure of the ultra-high-hardness 17Al alloy, especially the β-Mn/FCC Cu-rich interfaces.
characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with SAED and HRTEM

characterization_methods.key_findings: For the hardest 17Al sample (575 °C/6 h) the average nanoindentation hardness was 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa and the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn was 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: indentation depth 200 nm; test points spaced ≥ 5 µm apart; mechanically polished samples
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn and the overall micro-hardness of the hardest samples.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: EDS attached to the ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM / FEI Talos F200X TEM
characterization_methods.key_findings: The FCC phase is rich in Cu, depleted in Fe and Mn and slightly poor in Al while β-Mn is poor in Cu; for the hardest 17Al sample β-Mn contained Mn 36.2, Al 16.3 and Cu 2.6 at.%.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Elemental mapping and micro-area composition of β-Mn and Cu-rich particles
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine elemental partitioning (Cu-rich phase, β-Mn composition).

analytical_models.equation_role: Calculate K_IC from the elastic modulus, Vickers hardness, indentation load and average crack length

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Indentation load P = 9.8 N; average crack length c = 0.25 Σ(i=1..4) l_i (l_i = radial crack length from the indentation corners), as schematized in Fig. 1.
computational_details.simulation_method: Analytical indentation fracture-toughness model (Vickers indentation crack-length method)
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: K_IC values obtained for the hardest samples were 8.6 MPa·m^1/2 (15Al), 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 (17Al) and 3.5 MPa·m^1/2 (19Al), using average crack lengths of 18 µm, 22 µm and 35 µm respectively.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: FCC twins within the Cu-rich particles
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: SAED shows that the fine particles have an FCC crystalline structure with FCC twins frequently observed within the particles.

interfaces.interface_notes: The β-Mn/FCC-Cu-rich interface description derives from the general aged-state structure of the 17Al alloy; the TEM/HRTEM interface characterization (Fig. 12) was performed on the peak-hardness sibling condition 575 °C/6 h rather than on the 575 °C/10 h state of this sample.
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase

phases_present.morphology: matrix (uniform after complete α → β-Mn transformation)
fine precipitates distributed within the β-Mn
fine particles at the β-Mn interfaces

precipitates.distribution: matrix-forming after complete α → β-Mn transformation
within the β-Mn / at β-Mn interfaces

structures.overall_structure: After aging at 575 °C for 10 h the 17Al (Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu at.%) alloy consists of a β-Mn matrix: the α matrix is essentially fully transformed to β-Mn, and fine new BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates are present within the β-Mn.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: aged for 10 h then water quenched

unmapped_findings: The peak-hardness condition for the 17Al alloy is 575 °C/6 h (924.9 ± 25.8 HV), not the 575 °C/10 h state defined as this sample. Consequently the nanoindentation (H_Ave = 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa; intrinsic β-Mn hardness 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa), the β-Mn micro-area composition (Mn 36.2, Al 16.3, Cu 2.6 at.%), the average indentation crack length (22 µm), the calculated K_IC = 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 and the TEM interface characterization (Fig. 12) all refer to the 575 °C/6 h sibling sample, not to this 575 °C/10 h sample (b0060, b0061, b0058, figure_013, figure_014).

The XRD trace shown for the 17Al alloy (Fig. 10, red curve) was measured on the 575 °C/1 h condition, in which both α-Mn and β-Mn peaks were present, not on the 575 °C/10 h state of this sample (b0053, figure_010).
The maximum specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g is reported for the Fe-35.2Mn-15.0Al-5.2Cu (15Al) alloy; no specific hardness value is given for the 17Al alloy (b0008, b0077).

The volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich + BCC precipitates (4.7 %) quoted in the discussion corresponds to the 17Al alloy aged at 650 °C for 10 h (Vickers hardness 833.2 HV), a different aging condition from this sample (b0069).

The solution-treated baseline Vickers hardness of the 17Al alloy is 259.8 ± 1.5 HV (Table 3), which is the parent (proc_st-1100c-10min-oq) state from which this aged sample was produced (b0029, b0030).
Hardness contour analysis for the 17Al alloy identifies an optimal ultra-high-hardness aging window of about 550 °C–600 °C for this alloy (b0038).
